MR. FORTIN-PROTEST AGAINST STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON C.B.C. FRENCH NETWORK
speechtext:
Pursuant to Standing Order 17 (2), I have given notice to the Chair of a question of privilege I intended to raise at the beginning of the sitting, following the extremely serious statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last night on the C.B.C.'s French radio and television network, that is that members of the House of Commons are rather old fogies.
He stated moreover that parliament is an antiquated institution and on the whole, his statement suggested that he feels nothing good is done by parliament and that it is only a waste of time for which the members of the opposition are responsible.
To make it worse, the injustice results from the fact that the C.B.C.'s French network was not fair enough to ask for an account from a member of the opposition to counteract the Prime Minister's gratuitous and extremely serious statements.
In my opinion it is sheer dishonesty, a breach of the members' privileges and of the right to information of the Canadian people.

subtopic: MR. FORTIN-PROTEST AGAINST STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON C.B.C. FRENCH NETWORK
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MR. FORTIN-PROTEST AGAINST STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON C.B.C. FRENCH NETWORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is the essence of my question of privilege.
In view of the implications of the application of closure in accordance with standing order 33, considering that closure is seldom resorted to and that most often its application is odious, considering that those who resort to it must, from a parliamentary standpoint, be held responsible for the consequences, and considering that the people of Canada have a right to get accurate information, I say, Mr. Speaker, that the whole matter affects the right of the people of Canada to such accurate and fair information.
Indeed, Canadians must be informed of the fact that the opposition members are doing an honest job, not as dotards or simpletons but as responsible men. I suggest that the privileges of the people are being dangerously affected. It is the responsibility of every member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition to cast some light on this subject in order to bring the Right Hon. Prime Minister to express his opinions more specifically in respect of the disparagement campaign he has undertaken against the supreme, democratic institution which is parliament.
Mr. Speaker, as long as the rights and privileges of the representatives of Canadians in the House of Commons are not properly respected by the Right Hon. Prime Minister, we will have to conclude that this is a pure and simple belittling of parliament, made deliberately and with full awareness by the government, and I suggest this situation should not be tolerated by any parliamentarian worthy of the name.

I had a particular person in mind, Mr. Speaker. She is Miss Sandra Clouthier of R. R. 6, Pembroke, in my constituency. No driver's licence valid for extended meetings will be granted to women drivers who have not held previously such a licence valid for extended meetings.

Apparently this whole attempt to negotiate in the last four or five days has been an exercise which has now been proven futile. I must not impute motives. I am the last person in the house to do that, but I am wondering what kind of negotiations we have been having that we have reached the point at which we now find ourselves.
The result of this decision, if it is carried through, is as clear as can be. Proceedings during the next session of parliament will not be of the kind that they have been during this session. There will be confrontation and frustration. There will be work to rule, no more participating democracy. I appeal to the government even at this late hour to reconsider its position if it wants to retain the respect of the Canadian people who, as I say, believe in democracy.
The President of the Privy Council made reference to the proposals that the government placed before us during the course of our negotiations. The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) indicated the proposals made by his party during the same negotiations. There was agreement among us on some of these points. The particular position I put forward on behalf of this party was a very clear and direct one. My hon. friends opposite, at least through their house leader, were not prepared to accept it.

I think I have the right to state that we in this parliament did a good job last December. The job was not all done then, but it was an accumulation of four or five years' work. When we organized our legislative process the particular things we did were to downgrade slightly the importance of second reading and upgrade the importance of third reading, and to take the committee stage off the floor of the house and put it into standing committees. I think this was good and I think it has worked well. One of the reasons it has worked well is that we brought in something new, namely, the report stage at which it is possible to zero in on the points at issue and the points of contention.
I assert that one of the things which made the effect of new rules regarding the legislative process work was that the report stage included the right of all members to put down amendments to clauses of a bill that had been considered by a standing committee, or a committee of the whole. I think the experience we have had during the past six months demonstrates that this was a good rule.
The proposal now is that what we have achieved by our own common consent is to be frustrated and truncated and taken away by a rule that says no matter how many amendments there are it is within the power of the government to limit the debate on the entire report stage to two minutes and one day. I shall indicate in a moment or two what I intend to say about this through another point.
Let me make the point here that in our view one has to look at this legislative process in its broad perspective. One has to realize that second and third readings are important but not as important as they used to be, and that the report stage is supremely important. Therefore we proposed, and I did this at the meeting of the house leaders this morning with the full endorsation of the N.D.P. members of this house, that we would be willing to accept a time limitation even under some kind of a 75c on second and third readings. We suggested that the time limitation should not be less than three days at each of these stages. I think this is a pretty real offer for an opposition party to make.

I also want to congratulate the government and the minister for what they are doing to secure summer employment for students, at the urging of hon. members.
I also want to take this opportunity to praise several manpower centers that are doing commendable work to cope with the endemic state of unemployment, particularly in Quebec. Let us hope that those efforts will one day serve to render financially feasible what is physically possible.
I was sorry to hear that some students had refused employment on farms. Young university students like them could learn a whole lot of practical things, because even in university it is necessary to know that cows are milked twice a day. It is not necessary to wait until one becomes prime minister to learn that.
Every week, I draw the attention of the house to the problem of unemployment. As many other members, I receive a number of requests for employment from people between 35 and 50 years of age, who are unable to get any kind of work and are sometimes replaced by students. This problem should be considered seriously.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let us hope that with all the people of good will, we will work together in order to find a solution to the unemployment problem. Otherwise, socialism will take hold in Canada and I would fear that this would inevitably lead us to communism.

Mr. Speaker, I want to keep in mind your directive that we should not be too long at this stage.
I am sorry I cannot join the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) in congratulating the minister on anything he has stated to the house in his report. The statistics he gave are, in my view, extremely misleading. To make a sample study of Ottawa students is about as irrelevant to the situation across Canada as can be imagined. With the government and its various agencies in Ottawa, obviously students looking for work in this city are in the preferred place in Canada. This is an example of the kind of ill thought-out way in which this problem has been pursued by the minister and his department. They think they can satisfy parliament and the people by taking a sample of student employment in the one place where student employment is necessarily much easier to obtain. This is clearly misleading as to the true picture across Canada.
While some of the things undertaken by the department are obviously useful, as I have said on other occasions I am at a loss to know why these things take so long to implement.
Student Employment
It did not take a genius to know last winter that the problem of summer employment would be very serious this summer. It did not require a genius to know, in light of the policies pursued in a deliberate attempt to slow down the economy, there would be a general increase in unemployment and therefore more difficulties for students in the summer. Yet it was months before the minister could be persuaded to institute the inadequate program he has outlined today.

Therefore I cannot congratulate him or his department, although I am sure the officials are doing their best.
I also want to say I am getting thoroughly fed up with the attitude of ministers whenever any problem arises of emphasizing the fact that it is not their sole responsibility. We know that. No one in this house is unaware of the fact that there are things that have to be done by all parts of our society, both governmental and non-governmental. But the fact is that the Department of Manpower and Immigration is the only department of the federal government and the only over-all department of any government in Canada with the machinery to tackle the kind of problem that unemployment presents. It is nonsense to say, "It is not our sole responsibility". I wish ministers would stop singing this song as if it were a broken record. We know this government cannot do everything, but we also know that the responsibilities which are responsibilities of this government must be lived up to. The government cannot excuse itself by pointing out that other people have to do something as well.
I can only express the hope that the minister and the department will make a genuine, effective and nation-wide study of this problem so that if the government continues its policy of increasing unemployment generally the students will not be hurt even more than others. Even though students ought not to get any special consideration, surely we are dealing with a generation in this country which obviously represents our future technological and scientific progress and future leadership. Therefore the students at university and high school levels obviously need our attention, and in my opinion the government has failed to give them the kind of attention they deserve. I only hope that as a result of the department's studies somebody will wake up in the future a little earlier than the eleventh hour.

We are currently arranging to have some 18,000 students from 38 universities and community colleges questioned on their summer employment and jobhunting experiences. The sampling will represent approximately 5 per cent of Canada's post-secondary student population, and I am confident the results of this survey will be most helpful in developing future programs to find summer jobs for students.
As far as high school students are concerned, 102,768 have so far registered at Canada Manpower Centres; as these students have only just become available for employment I cannot at this point give any reliable statistics on placements.
Another aspect of our student summer employment program has been to intensify efforts to encourage farmers to hire students for available agricultural jobs and to alert students to these job opportunities. Many farmers have responded positively to our canvassing but 1 must note that some students are still reluctant to take this type of work.
By the end of June, some 6,937 students had been placed in farm jobs, the majority being pre or secondary level students; at the same time there were 2,653 active or deferred vacancies for farm jobs recorded in our C.M.C. files. Up to June 30, approximately 3,000 students had refused summer jobs in agriculture.
I am hopeful, though, particularly this month and in August, that students who have not found jobs will accept summer employment in agriculture. In this connection members will recall that this year I have reduced by 50 per cent the number of foreign students coming to Canada to work on farms; this was done so that more of the jobs could be filled by Canadian students.
I assure hon. members of my concern about the student summer employment situation in Canada, always bearing in mind two important considerations. One is that any federal program of this kind must be studied in relation to resources and that services for one group of individuals-in this case, students- must not be disproportionate to services expected by other Canadian citizens who have employment difficulties.
